narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 54.6% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your third-year class ranking had the strongest influence, pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. Placing in the second decile is well below the average of roughly sixth-decile performance among students who were accepted, signaling that your later academic performance was weaker than most successful applicants.

Your undergraduate GPA came next. At 2.60 it is noticeably lower than the 3.23 average of accepted students, which pulled the prediction toward passing. However, this positive effect was not large enough to overcome the negative impact of your class rank.

Your high family income also worked in your favor, making success slightly more likely. Among accepted students only about 9% come from high-income backgrounds, so this is an uncommon but helpful factor; yet again, it could not offset the dominant influence of your third-year ranking.

Taken together, these academic signals led the model to conclude your risk of failing the bar was too high for admission. To improve your chances on a future application, focus on raising your class rank in subsequent years and consider retaking courses or seeking additional academic support to strengthen your GPA before reapplying.
